<reflection>
- The previous experiment (S=2.0, cat=0.15, P=0.5) successfully penalized models with strong product inhibition/deactivation (M12, M17) and certain substrate/free-catalyst deactivation pathways (M11, M9, M20), pushing them to the bottom of the likelihood rankings.
- However, the top models (M8, M6, M13, M3, M2, M1) remain highly degenerate, with NLL scores within ~0.4 units of each other. 
- My aim to broadly separate the models was partially achieved, but the models are currently compensating for the S=2.0, cat=0.15 conditions by adjusting their rate constants. The top models now primarily differ in their dependence on catalyst concentration (first-order activation in M6/M8 vs. second-order dimerization/deactivation in M2/M3/M13).
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To break the degeneracy between first-order catalyst mechanisms (M1, M6, M8) and second-order catalyst mechanisms (M2, M3, M13), we need to probe the system at a very low catalyst concentration. 
By setting the catalyst concentration to 0.005 (a 10- to 30-fold decrease from previous runs), second-order interactions (which scale with $[cat]^2$) will be drastically reduced. Models relying on dimerization or bimolecular deactivation (M2, M3, M13) will predict a non-linear scaling of the reaction rate across the three experiments, whereas first-order models (M1, M6, M8) will scale linearly. 
Additionally, by using the maximum substrate concentration (S=5.0), we will saturate the catalyst, pushing the equilibrium strongly toward the `catS` intermediate and minimizing free `cat`. This will simultaneously test for substrate-induced inhibition/deactivation (M7, M16) and `catS`-specific deactivation (M14, M18) under conditions where free `cat` is minimized, providing a highly orthogonal constraint to the previous experiments.
</hypothesis>
